summary: Specifies how to use the SEED encryption algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), adding it to the optional symmetric algorithms through two classes of object identifiers.

eli5.summary: It lets a secure-message format use the Korean SEED code, with name tags to say so.

subtitle: How to plug Korea's SEED block cipher into CMS for encrypting content and wrapping keys.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) needs identifiers and processing rules before a new cipher such as SEED can be used for content or key encryption.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4010 defines two object identifiers, one for SEED in CBC mode to encrypt content and one for SEED key wrap, reuses the AES key wrap procedure with SEED, and sets the S/MIME capability encoding.
tldr.outcome: CMS and S/MIME agents can negotiate and use SEED as an optional symmetric algorithm, with the security considerations of CMS and AES key wrap applying.

today: RFC 4010 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2005. According to the metadata it has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on RFC 4009, which describes the SEED algorithm.

sections.title: SEED and Its Role in CMS
sections.content:
This RFC gives the conventions for using the SEED encryption algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS, RFC 3852 and RFC 3370) for content and key encryption. It supplies the object identifiers (OIDs) and processing steps. SEED itself is specified in RFC 4009.

The RFC describes SEED as a symmetric algorithm developed by KISA (Korea Information Security Agency) and a group of experts since 1998. Block size and key length are both 128 bits, and it has a 16-round Feistel structure. It is described as needing less memory than other algorithms, which suits restricted environments such as mobile devices and smart cards, and as widely used in South Korea for electronic commerce and financial services. Per the text, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 27 and Japan's CRYPTREC evaluated it and consider it cryptographically secure.
sections.eli5: SEED is a lock-and-key code from Korea that works on chunks of data and is small enough to run on phones and smart cards. This RFC shows how to use it in secure messages.

sections.title: Content Encryption With SEED-CBC
sections.content:
SEED is added to the symmetric content encryption algorithms of CMS (RFC 3370). The CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) mode has the OID id-seedCBC, which is { iso(1) member-body(2) korea(410) kisa(200004) algorithm(1) seedCBC(4) }.

The AlgorithmIdentifier parameters field MUST be present and MUST hold the initialization vector (IV), defined as SeedIV ::= OCTET STRING (SIZE(16)). Plain text is padded as described in Section 6.3 of RFC 3852.
sections.eli5: To lock the message itself, you pick the SEED-CBC name tag and attach a 16-byte random starter value so the lock works the same way for both sides.

sections.title: Key Encryption and the Key Wrap Algorithm
sections.content:
SEED can also encrypt a SEED content-encryption key (CEK) with a SEED key-encryption key (KEK). The OID is id-npki-app-cmsSeed-wrap. Its parameter MUST be absent, because the wrap procedure itself defines how and when to use an IV. Generating and distributing KEKs is out of scope.

The wrap and unwrap procedures follow the AES key wrap algorithm of RFC 3394 (its Sections 2.2.1 and 2.2.2) with AES replaced by SEED. The plaintext is n 64-bit blocks of key data, the ciphertext is n+1 blocks, and the process runs s = 6n steps. Each step encrypts a 128-bit input made by joining two 64-bit values, then splits the output back into two 64-bit parts. The RFC gives both a register-shifting and an index-based version, which produce identical results.
sections.eli5: To protect a secret key, you wrap it inside another key. The wrapping repeats the same shuffle many times, six times per piece of key, until the secret is thoroughly scrambled.

sections.title: The Integrity Check Value
sections.content:
The initial value assigned to the integrity register A[0] doubles as an integrity check. When unwrapping, the recovered A[0] is compared with the expected value. A match means the key is accepted; otherwise the key is rejected and an error is returned.

The default value is the hexadecimal constant A6A6A6A6A6A6A6A6. If unwrapping yields it, the chance the key data is corrupt is 2^-64. Any other result must return an error and no key data. Alternative initial values are allowed for larger key management systems, and the RFC notes that NIST is expected to define them in future publications, per RFC 3394.
sections.eli5: The wrapped key has a secret stamp inside. If the stamp looks right after unwrapping, the key is fine. If not, you throw it away.

sections.title: S/MIME Capabilities
sections.content:
An S/MIME client SHOULD announce its supported cryptographic functions with the SMIMECapabilities signed attribute (RFC 3851), which MUST be signed by the client. OIDs SHOULD be grouped by function and MUST be ordered by preference.

A client that supports SEED for symmetric encryption MUST include the SEED OID in the symmetric category, with the parameter SeedSMimeCapability, which is NULL. The capability MUST be DER-encoded as 30 0C 06 08 2A 83 1A 8C 9A 44 01 04 05 00.

If local policy requires SEED, both sender and receiver must support it and it must be configured as the preferred symmetric algorithm.
sections.eli5: A mail program can tell others which codes it understands. If it knows SEED, it lists SEED with a fixed byte pattern so others recognize it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC uses SEED only to encrypt CMS content and the symmetric key that protects it, with the other mechanisms unchanged. The security considerations of the CMS specifications and of the AES key wrap algorithm therefore apply. The text also states that no security problem has been found on SEED, citing the CRYPTREC evaluation.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is added to the risks. The same safety rules as the existing secure-message format apply, and no weakness in SEED has been found.

items.title: id-seedCBC
items.text: Content encryption in CBC mode. Parameters MUST hold a 16-byte IV.

items.title: id-npki-app-cmsSeed-wrap
items.text: Key encryption using key wrap. Parameters MUST be absent.
